articles.title_orig: Dow futures rise 300 points as Nvidia rebounds, inflation data comes in light: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures rise 300 points as Nvidia rebounds, inflation data comes in light: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite fell on Friday as Nvidia shares added to their recent losses, though the index still headed for a winning week alongside the other two major averages.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 1.7%, while the S&P 500 slid 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded down 70 points, or 0.1%.
Equities initially popped after October's producer price index reading — a measure of wholesale inflation — showed an increase of 0.3% on the month. Economists polled by Dow Jones had seen headline PPI rising 0.4%.
However, the report also showed producer prices gaining 6.5% from 12 months earlier — the biggest annual advance since November 2022.
"Today's PPI data — which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high — is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management.
"We believe the Fed will raise rates 25 bps in December," he also said, adding that he considers January a "live meeting."
Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market for another day. The stock fell more than 4% Friday, extending the more than 4% drop it saw in the previous session. The pressure came after the exit of the scandal-hit chipmaker's founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
HSBC downgraded the chipmaker Friday to hold, believing that the stock will languish until the company lays out a permanent succession plan.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all pulled back on Thursday after Huang stepped down from his post following reported extramarital affairs , including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress , who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages are heading for weekly advances. The Nasdaq is up more than 1%, while the S&P 500 and the Dow are poised to post an almost 2% jump.
Bitcoin traded below $70,000 for the first time since August in a risk-off move, falling as low as $67,632.68, its lowest level since Aug. 19, according to Coin Metrics.
Its recent weakness coincides with strength in the U.S. dollar. On Friday, the dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold – despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling and, this week, more than $1 billion in leveraged bitcoin liquidations, per CoinGlass. The declines began in late October, as concerns over AI valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off, and were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite gave up their early gains and moved into negative territory in morning trading on Friday.
The broad market index was down 0.4%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 0.7%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average , however, rose 43 points, or 0.1%.
The three major averages began Friday's session in the green.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 208 points, or 0.4%, just after 9:30 a.m. ET. The S&P 500 rose 0.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 0.1%.
The 10-year Treasury yield remained over 5% on Friday after October's producer price index came in slightly less than expected.
The yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose nearly 4 basis points to 5.14%.
Read the full story here .
Wholesale inflation rose less than expected last month, a welcome sign for investors worried about high inflation driving expectations for a Fed rate hike.
The producer price index rose 0.3% in October on a month-over-month basis. Economists polled by Dow Jones expected PPI to have risen 0.4%.
However, on an unadjusted basis, the index for final demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022.
Palo Alto Networks is likely to regain ground as companies bump up their security budgets, according to KeyBanc.
The bank upgraded the cybersecurity stock to overweight from sector weight. It also put a $380 price target on shares, implying nearly 18% upside from Thursday's close.
"We are upgrading shares of PANW to Overweight as we expect security budgets to accelerate through 2027, Palo a leading beneficiary of the trend toward consolidation with strong product offerings in key areas to secure AI and defend against the accelerated AI threat environment, and Palo out-executing many of its cyber peers," analyst Eric Heath said Thursday in a note to clients.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making premarket moves.
— Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert
Bitcoin dropped 3% to trade below $70,000 for the first time since August. The largest cryptocurrency by market cap was last at $69,231.05 and was on pace for its sixth consecutive weekly decline.
Nvidia shares rebounded in pre-market trading on Friday, with the stock adding around 2.3% by 5:30 a.m. ET. It followed a decline of just over 4% in Thursday's regular trading session as investors weighed the company's future without its longtime leader Jensen Huang.
More broadly, stocks in the semiconductor space were mixed ahead of the final opening bell of the week.
AMD shares were last seen trading 2.6% lower. Broadcom fell 2.8%, while Intel , Micron and Lam Research each lost around 0.9%.
Amid a volatile week for Nvidia stock, some of its rivals had earlier emerged as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval.
Microsoft shares were 3% lower in premarket trade at 4:35 a.m. ET, as the company's engineers continued to grapple with server issues that caused a widespread outage of its Outlook service, disrupting businesses, governments and the general public around the world.
Outlook was inaccessible via app or browser throughout the Asian business day and into Europe's morning, with related services also impacted. Connectivity issues began around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday, hitting hundreds of thousands of U.S. Microsoft users.
The company said at 4:14 a.m. ET on Friday that it was seeing "early signs of stabilization" but that service would be "variable," and it was working to preserve mail delayed during the recovery process. It added it was not aware if "malicious activity" was the cause of the incident.
Shares of Richemont are on track for their worst day since July 2023, even after the luxury conglomerate posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Friday.
Swiss-listed shares were down 6.8% in morning trading.
Sales rose 13% at constant exchange rates in the quarter ended September, while its important jewellery business, which includes Cartier and Van Cleef, grew 14%.
Results exceeded expectations; however, they marked a slowdown from the previous quarter, when total sales grew by 20% and jewellery grew by 24%.
The luxury sector has seen a prolonged slump amid higher pricing and overall softer demand, especially in China. Richemont said sales in mainland China were down about 3% in the first half of the fiscal year.
Luxury peers LVMH , Gucci-owner Kering and Hermes all traded lower in morning trading Friday.
Nvidia shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of at least two affairs.
It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower.

articles.title_orig: China warns against new U.S. export controls on chips in wake of Nvidia's Huang scandal
articles.title_zh: China warns against new U.S. export controls on chips in wake of Nvidia's Huang scandal
articles.content_orig:
China warned the United States on Friday against imposing additional controls on exports of semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding AI chip giant Nvidia and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang.
China "has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party's interests," foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular press briefing when asked about calls from U.S. lawmakers to impose more limits on exports of chip equipment to China.
"China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their respective heads of state and maintain the stable development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations," Mao said.
Jensen Huang — who resigned Thursday — has admitted to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. They're not related.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Jensen Huang contributed to a lack of oversight by the federal agency over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS News has learned . The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Last month, the New York Times reported that about a year ago, President Trump was briefed on intelligence that suggested that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset and that she had grown close to Jensen Huang and the president decided not to do anything with the information.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said there's a growing consensus in Congress on further tightening controls on chip exports to China.
According to the Times , U.S. officials circulated a memo last spring citing intelligence alleging that Alice Huang was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, its main intelligence service.
Beijing has rejected the allegations and said on Thursday that they are a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" to stop China advancing in artificial intelligence technology .

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed's vacant offices raise questions about ties to Nvidia and China
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed's vacant offices raise questions about ties to Nvidia and China
articles.content_orig:
The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security . On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned .
In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.
And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.
Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.
Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In a statement Thursday, Megaspeed said it "takes its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously" and that it's "committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government."
The company also said that it "has cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority."
President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related).
Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter , and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship.
Nvidia's board said Sunday that it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," its statement said.
However, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust Jensen Huang, a development that was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
China expert Jacqueline Deal said that Nvidia's advanced AI chips could have ended up with the Chinese military. Deal, who is an adviser to State Armor, a nonprofit that studies global security threats, told CBS News, "If allegations are true, who will be fired? Nvidia has a compliance team that may have failed utterly."
She also questioned the effectiveness of the U.S. Commerce Department, which has jurisdiction over export controls that may have been bypassed, potentially giving the Chinese military access to the world's most advanced chips.
Here's what we now know about Megaspeed:
It is a major Nvidia customer. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence equipment and processors over the last three years.
In 2025, Megaspeed International faced an investigation by Singapore police for alleged breaches of local laws, but no details have emerged about the probe, according to The Straits Times.
"Megaspeed International is a premier business partner of NVIDIA, strategically positioned in the Asia Pacific region," according to its LinkedIn profile, which claims it has between 201 and 500 employees. Three years ago it listed between two and 10 employees, according to the South China Morning Post.
Megaspeed International did not reply to a request for comment. It posted an "official statement" on its website addressing what it called "misleading information" and "incorrect insinuations" accusing it of involvement in illegal chip transfers.
"We want to be absolutely clear over the past six months our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia and NVIDIA," said the message, which also appeared on the company's LinkedIn page.
"These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said.
But in a statement on Thursday, the company said it had "retained a leading U.S. law firm to ... independently verify its export control compliance practices. Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws."
Megaspeed was originally incorporated in 2015 under the name 7Road International, a subsidiary of a Chinese developer of popular video games and mobile apps based in Shenzhen, China, according to corporate filings.
Huang Le Limited, a shell company in the British Virgin Islands, acquired 7Road International in March 2023. Huang Le is the Chinese name of Alice Huang.
That same month, 7Road International was renamed Megaspeed International, and Huang became its managing director. The company also launched a subsidiary called Speedmatrix.
By the end of October 2023, Huang and another Megaspeed director, Cang Yang, resigned from the company after it was bought up by a firm called Swiftdata, whose director is based in China, documents show.
But there's some indication Huang may still be affiliated with the company. Culper Research, an activist short-selling firm , published a 40-page report on Nvidia in May that cited Megaspeed employees who said Huang was still running the company.
The report also raised some concern about Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, stating, "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national."
Megaspeed lists its headquarters office address on the seventh floor of the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore, a glass office tower in Singapore's central business district.
When the Straits Times and The New York Times visited the Singapore offices around the same time late last year, they found little or no staff working. The Straits Times said the door was locked, and the Times found just two people in its office on a workday.
Megaspeed has an Australian subsidiary on the 10th floor of a commercial and retail tower in the heart of Sydney's central business district. Forty other businesses are on the same floor, and space in the building can be rented for as little as $17 per day, Australia's ABC News reported. Corporate filings name Shanghai-born Kai Kang, a 29-year-old newspaper vendor, as the director, according to Australian news reports. But Kang's newsstand is in Northern Victoria, over 400 miles from Sydney. Kang's father told Australia's ABC News this week that he had never heard of Megaspeed.

articles.title_orig: Lutnick should have prevented the diversion of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, critics charge
articles.title_zh: Lutnick should have prevented the diversion of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, critics charge
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Nvidia's ousted CEO Jensen Huang contributed to the federal agency's lack of oversight over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS News has learned.
Before President Trump nominated Lutnick to lead the Commerce Department, Lutnick was the chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York investment bank which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time.
Lutnick developed a warm relationship with Huang, who resigned Thursday as reports of a growing number of affairs caused new uncertainty about the world's dominant AI chipmaker. One of Huang's alleged relationships was with Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen Huang), who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy. She ran Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that became one of Nvidia's biggest customers for AI chips and is suspected of illegally shipping Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to Chinese entities, circumventing a U.S. ban.
As commerce secretary, Lutnick took the helm of an agency responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals.
One way the Commerce Department keeps this information and technology out of the hands of China and other adversaries is by putting foreign companies and individuals on its Entity List . This restricts their ability to access U.S. technology products, and inclusion on the list means that the department believes there's a risk that the entity is involved in activities that are contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.
In 2024, under the Biden administration, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security launched an investigation into Nvidia's chip sales to Megaspeed to determine whether they were being redirected to China. But according to The New York Times , the probe was abruptly transferred to the Department of Justice. The Justice Department would not comment about the investigation.
The Commerce Department has not added a company to the Entity List since October 2025.
Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over the Commerce Department's failure to place Megaspeed on the Entity List, Axios reported.
Chris McGuire, an expert on China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said, "The real scandal here is the lack of enforcement of export controls."
He added that the Commerce Department had known for as long as a year that Megaspeed was being run by a woman who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy, "and they did nothing." The New York Times reported that about a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed on intelligence that suggested that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset and that she had grown close to Jensen Huang.
"Either Lutnick doesn't know how to do his job or he is protecting Huang," McGuire said.
The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.
On Thursday, after Jensen Huang's resignation became public, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, called on Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, to "explain why they have not closed export control loopholes." Kessler is the undersecretary who led the Commerce Department's probe into Megaspeed.
Warren urged the two to "act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In March, Warren wrote to Lutnick to demand the "immediate pausing" of all export licenses of Nvidia chips destined for China.
Questions about Lutnick's own relationship with Chinese state companies have further complicated the ongoing Nvidia crisis.
A financial services firm Lutnick ran, BGC Group, had a 33% stake in a joint venture with China Credit Trust, a Chinese state-owned company whose largest shareholder is the China People's Insurance Company, another state enterprise.
Another firm he ran, Cantor Fitzgerald, is still overseen by his two eldest sons. That firm helped several Chinese companies go public in the U.S. Cantor Fitzgerald was also a key investor in Satellogic, a satellite company that is under contract with a Chinese data science company, Zhong Ke Guang Qi Space, until 2033.
His close China ties emerged as a topic at his Senate confirmation hearing last year. Senators questioned whether he could be unduly influenced by Chinese officials, and how he would safeguard U.S. technology.
Sen. Maria Cantwell, a Democrat from Washington state, grilled Lutnick on potential conflicts of interest with respect to his investments in Chinese companies, and Cantor Fitzgerald's financial interest in Tether, a cryptocurrency company with a large footprint in China.
Other senators asked about how he would safeguard U.S. technology from the Chinese Communist Party.
"How will you address different threats that we see coming from the CCP within these information and technology markets?" asked GOP Sen. Deb Fischer, of Nebraska.
Lutnick promised to be vigilant against threats from China.
"I take a very jaundiced view of China," he said in response to Fischer. "I think they only care about themselves and seek harm to us, and so we need to protect ourselves."
Before he was sworn in as commerce secretary in February 2025, Lutnick resigned from all of his corporate leadership posts, transferring his business empire to his children.
Since his tenure as commerce secretary began, Lutnick and his family's net worth doubled to $7.3 billion, thanks to his indirect stake in Tether, according to Forbes , which valued his holding in Tether at $5.4 billion. The stake, worth $1.7 billion in early 2025, has more than tripled in value.
"Can we be confident that he is looking out for the public interest?" asked Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "What's going on with him raises a lot of red flags."
Lutnick's friendship with Jensen Huang may also be problematic, Clark told CBS News.
Huang met Lutnick soon after Lutnick began his term as commerce secretary, Huang told podcaster Joe Rogan last year.
"He started our conversation with, 'Jensen, this is Secretary Lutnick,'" said Huang. "'I just want to let you know that you're a national treasure. Nvidia is a national treasure. And whenever you need access to the president, the administration, you call us.'"
Huang added that every time he called the commerce secretary's office, "if I want to get something off my chest, express some concern, they're always available."
Huang also visited with Mr. Trump. He attended a $1 million-per-person dinner at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025. At that time, Huang tried to convince Mr. Trump to lift restrictions on the company's less advanced H20 chip sales to China, according to The New York Times . Less than three months later, in July 2025, Mr. Trump lifted the restrictions. Nvidia's most advanced chip, the Blackwell, still cannot be sold directly to China.
In July 2025, Lutnick posted a photo to Instagram showing Huang in his trademark black leather jacket standing in the Oval Office next to Mr. Trump, who was seated at his desk. Lutnick is also in the photo along with other visitors.
"Great to meet in the Oval Office with Jensen Huang on the very day Nvidia crossed $4 trillion in market cap," the post said.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Secretary Bessent on if any Nvidia chips went to China through Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Treasury Secretary Bessent on if any Nvidia chips went to China through Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's spy-sex scandal .
But the Commerce Department is in charge, "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's " Squawk Box ."
The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed.
Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.
Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room.
Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room."
But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s."
"And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive that U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy.
Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.
Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down."
"The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"
"I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said.
This is breaking news. Please check back for updates.

SpaceX is counting down to make history with the launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13 , with liftoff scheduled for 5:45 p.m. EDT (2245 GMT) at Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land both Starship Ship and Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever full recovery of an orbital rocket and spacecraft, if successful.
Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which will also deliver 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.
Flight 15 livestream | SpaceX | Starship | Starship V3 explained
Good morning, Space Fans, it is launch day for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 and the world's largest rocket is now hours away from attempting its first double landing test flight. Liftoff remains on target for today, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) from SpaceX's Starbase launch site in South Texas. You'll be able to w atch the Starship Flight 15 launch on this page, as well as on Space.com's homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace . Our live webcast will begin at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT) .
Last night, SpaceX rolled the Ship 42 upper stage out to the Starship launch pad and stacked it atop its Super Heavy booster. The Ship's number was accompanied by a fun sci-fi message - "Don't Panic" - in a nod to the Hitchhiker's Guide To The Galaxy books by Douglas Adams. Elon Musk's Tesla bore the same message when SpaceX launched it into space on the first Falcon Heavy mission.
Space.com's Josh Dinner is on site at Starbase and will be providing updates as possible from Starbase, which we'll share here as they're received.
Here's an update from Josh from the launch pad:
A post shared by Space.com (@spacedotcom)
SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 is the 15th test flight of Starship, the world's largest and most powerful rocket. SpaceX has designed the rocket to be fully reusable, and has landed its massive Super Heavy first stage booster several times.
Flight 15 is SpaceX's first attempt to land both the Super Heavy booster and its Ship upper stage by returning them to their launch pad and catching them in the pad's metal "Chopstick" arms. The landings will be about 22 hours apart, with Super Heavy landing minutes after launch and the Ship upper stage returning to Starbase on Saturday afternoon.
We'll be updating this page throughout the day with news from Josh, SpaceX and Starbase for this unprecedented 22.5-hour test flight. Here's our full timeline for SpaceX Starship Flight 15 .
SpaceX is now less than 24 hours from the planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission , with liftoff on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). The test flight will attempt land both the Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 and its Ship 42 upper stage.
Because the mission will last 22.5 hours, Starship will likely be visible in the night sky to stargazers hoping to see the giant spacecraft in orbit. Space.com's Skywatching Writer Anthony Wood has a great guide on how to see Starship in the night sky.
"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station , but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," our skywatching columnist Joe Rao told Wood.
Check out the full story: SpaceX's Starship megarocket will launch to orbit on Nov. 13. Will you be able to spot it in the night sky?
STARBASE, Texas — We are one day until launch of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15, and Space.com is onsite here in Texas prepping cameras and coverage.
Liftoff is currently targeted for tomorrow (Nov. 13), during a 75-minute window opening at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT).
This flight could be a historic one for SpaceX and the space industry. For the first time, SpaceX will attempt to catch both stages of its massive Starship rocket — Super Heavy just minutes after launch, and the Ship upper stage roughly 22 hours later, following several orbits around Earth.
I'll be covering the action from here in Texas, so stay tuned to Space.com for updates as we count down to liftoff!
Happy Wednesday, Space Fans. We are now T-2 days away from SpaceX's planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test mission, so I wanted to take a moment to give you a run down on what to expect.
Today, you can read my full guide to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch here , which goes over what time and where to watch the launch online. Liftoff is on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 4:45 p.m. CST, which is 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). Flight 15 will mark the first time SpaceX will attempt to land and catch both the Super Heavy booster (which it has done several times) and the Ship from orbit.
If successful, it will be the first full recovery of an entire orbital rocket from space.
Hello, Space Fans, and welcome to our coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight , the first ever to attempt twin landings of the Starship Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage.
SpaceX has officially set the launch date for Flight 15 for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EDT (2145 GMT) . That puts launch just about 3 days away and Space.com will provide live coverage of the potentially historic flight, the first full recovery of an orbital rocket.
Space.com Spaceflight Writer Josh Dinner will be reporting live from near SpaceX's Starbase , Texas site for the launch, with myself (Tariq Malik), Spaceflight and Tech Editor Mike Wall and other team members tracking the flight remotely for you here. articles.title_orig: Europe pushes for a seat at Ukraine peace talks‌ but lacks a unified voice
articles.title_zh: Europe pushes for a seat at Ukraine peace talks‌ but lacks a unified voice
articles.content_orig:
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. Now they finally expect to get one, and they don’t know who should sit in it.
“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said on Thursday.
Mr. Kushner’s dig reflected a harsh — and, for Europe, potentially embarrassing — reality that internal divisions could cost European officials time and influence. Mr. Kushner and his fellow U.S. negotiator, Steve Witkoff, pushed this week to add Europe to the talks after Russia insisted during discussions in the United Arab Emirates that postwar security in Europe be a topic of negotiation.
Russian negotiators made it clear during the talks with Ukraine and the United States that as a condition of ending the war, they want Europe to change how it protects itself. Russia has a record of pushing to pare back NATO operations near its border.
European officials have rejected those suggestions, insisting that the continent, not the Kremlin, decides its security.

articles.title_orig: Commerce Secretary Lutnick agreed to testify on Nvidia's AI chip sales to China
articles.title_zh: Commerce Secretary Lutnick agreed to testify on Nvidia's AI chip sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.
Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.
Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.
The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."
Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.
There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough
Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."
In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.
Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.
Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Huang exit and US scrutiny imperil $3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Huang exit and US scrutiny imperil $3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.
On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.77%, nearly 6% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
Tech stocks slumped Thursday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 0.3% as markets digested the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Thursday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt  lingers.
It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.
Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.
CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.75% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped 18% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.
It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.
"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.
"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."
"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."
Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.
The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.
"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."
— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Would You Get Stoned With The Scythians?
articles.title_zh: Would You Get Stoned With The Scythians?
articles.content_orig:
9:00 AM EST on November 13, 2026
It's just like they told you it would happen in D.A.R.E. You have been miraculously, tragically transported 2,800 years back in time, in the land that is now the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia. The site will be eventually called Tunnug 1 by the archaeologists who excavate it in 2017. But that is the future, and this is the present, meaning 800 B.C. You have come to sit with the Scythians, nomads who roamed the Eurasian steppes on horseback. You have even glimpsed their warrior-king, whose long and stately braids make him seem like a pretty cool guy. Also, he's smoking. Suddenly the warrior-king glimpses you back, his reddish eyes glinting in the firelight. He leans over to you, whispers something inscrutable in an Eastern Iranic language, and extends in his grizzled hands an ancient joint, leaving you with only one question: Would you smoke that shit?
There are, to be certain, pros and cons. But one thing is clear, per a paper published recently in the journal Science : the Scythians were definitely using cannabis to get high. The analysis, led by Fabio-haired University of Bern archaeologist Gino Caspari, represents the earliest definitive evidence of humans consuming marijuana as a psychoactive drug, which was previously only traced back 2,500 years ago where Sogdian mourners once lit up in the ancient Jirzankal Cemetery in what is now western China.
It's only fitting that marijuana hails from one of the highest places in the world: the eastern Tibetan Plateau, also known as the Roof of the World. The plant evolved around 28 million years ago, and as early as 4,000 years ago Chinese farmers cultivated the plant for rope, clothing, and paper, per Science . But it is harder to tell when in the archaeological record ancient people first became gone off that loud. Wild weed, the ancestors of the domesticated kind, has only a little tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the plant's intoxicating compound. Some researchers confirmed this when they tried to smoke wild weed and felt nothing, also per Science . (It is unclear if these particular researchers are also the authors of the paper, who described cannabis as an "illicit" substance.)
But scholars have long suspected that Scythians were hotboxing, quite literally, in part due to the testimony of the Greek historian and geographer Herodotus, who was known to sensationalize his accounts (he once wrote of dog-sized ants that harvested gold). Herodotus recorded the following description of the nomads' funerary practices, per this translation of The Histories by George Campbell Macaulay:
The Scythians then take the seed of this hemp and creep under the felt coverings, and then they throw the seed upon the stones which have been heated red-hot: and it burns like incense and produces a vapour so thick that no vapour-bath in Hellas would surpass it: and the Scythians being delighted with the vapour-bath howl like wolves.
Let's go back to the warrior-king for a second. It's true that we don't know for sure if he's a warrior-king, but he would become one of the people buried at the center of the royal burial mound at Tunnug 1, whose tombs contained gold jewelry, statues of animals, weapons, and, most importantly, nearly a thousand whole cannabis seeds that appear to have been deposited around 2,800 years ago. This is where the archaeologists found strands of human hair, which had been preserved in two pristine braids. When they tested the hair, they found traces of cannabinol, or CBN, which is a byproduct of THC. Archaeology is almost always accompanied by some degree of uncertainty, but this mound of evidence—weed seeds and weed in hair—makes the case for stoner Scythians fairly open-and-shut.
Some outside researchers are skeptical, including forensic toxicologist Volker Auwärter, who told the AP that he found the hair analysis "scientifically weak," as well as a commenter called Fabio who wrote "Drugs of choice back then was opium." But many scientists appear to be convinced, such as William Taylor, an archaeologist at the University of Colorado Boulder. "It’s easy to look at this stuff and say, ‘Oh, the Scythians toked the reefer,'" Taylor told Scientific American . "But in fact, it is a tremendously powerful snapshot into an interconnected world in which the people and cultures of the steppe were starting to shape life on both ends of a massive continent."
Tremendously powerful snapshots, sure, but let's return to the fact that the Scythians toked the reefer. I feel an important question that has been lost amid the buzz of the discovery: What would it be like get smoked out by the Scythians? I've taken the liberty of gathering some pros and cons.
Option 1: 420 B.C. Blaze It
If you were transported all the way back in time to 800 B.C. and offered a joint by a Scythian warrior-king, there are many good reasons to take at least one puff. You could imagine the punishment that might follow refusing a king. It might be nice to take the edge off 2,800 years of time travel. But the most important, I think, is that it would be real loser shit to say no.
But more seriously. The Scythians were famous for their " animal style ," which is not the ancestor of an In-N-Out secret menu item—which I'm sure a smoking Scythian would have loved—but rather a stylized artistic tradition that rendered highly stylized animals in gold, bronze, and bone. What kind of altered mental state might produce such a fantastic deer?
Imagine the small talk you could have with a roving band of Scythians. Sure, they spoke a group of ancient Iranic languages that you would probably not understand. Perhaps they would have spoken of their gods, such as the hearth-goddess Tabití . Perhaps they would have told you how to find one of the rivers on the steppe, such as the Borysthénēs , where you could find some kapa , or fish. You would smile and nod to all of this if you were high. Then maybe they would have offered you some cheese called hippákē .
If Herodotus is to be believed, smoking with a Scythian would probably not have involved a joint or a pipe, but rather a communal inhalation of smoke. But Herodotus makes this sound like a real good time. I, too, would like to throw the hemp seed upon the red-hot stones and howl like a wolf at the delights of the vapor-bath! Because the weed was found inside the burial mound, the researchers suspect that it may have played a role in a ritual funerary practice, perhaps for some kind of religious experience. But there is another, more sinister reason the Scythians may have wanted you to, in Taylor's particular parlance, toke the reefer.
Option 2: Say No To Scythians
Although the wooden tombs of Tunnug 1 contained the graves of important individuals buried in coffins made of tree trunks and logs, these wooden structures were topped with what is often called a "spectral cavalcade," a fancy word for a heap of sacrificed horses and humans. Horses, sure, but humans? We must return once more to our friend Herodotus, who described in great detail the spectral cavalcade practice that follows a king's burial in The Histories :
Afterwards, when the year comes round again, they do as follows:—they take the most capable of the remaining servants,—and these are native Scythians, for those serve him whom the king himself commands to do so, and his servants are not bought for money,—of these attendants then they strangle fifty and also fifty of the finest horses; and when they have taken out their bowels and cleansed the belly, they fill it with chaff and sew it together again.
On the horses they put bridles and bits, and stretch the bridles tight in front of them and then tie them up to pegs: and of the fifty young men who have been strangled they mount each one upon his horse, having first run a straight stake through each body along by the spine up to the neck; and a part of this stake projects below, which they fasten into a socket made in the other stake that runs through the horse. articles.title_orig: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
articles.content_orig:
Despite losing its majority in last month’s parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is still in power in a caretaker capacity.
That will continue until a new governing majority is formed – a process that could take months as Israel’s opposition struggles to form a coalition.
And while he may be politically weakened, Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran , despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and the politicians vying to replace him.
But does Netanyahu’s caretaker government actually have the authority to send Israel back to war, and how would such a move be received at home?
Officially, Israel’s caretaker government has the same authority as a regular government. Article 30 of the country’s Basic Law states that an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place.
However, Israel’s Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent – a principle known as the “duty of restraint”.
In practice, Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as “urgent and in the national interest”, Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University, London, and the author of “Israel’s Occupation”, told Al Jazeera.
Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told the Reuters news agency that security issues generally are “the clearest exception” to a caretaker government’s duty of restraint.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset [parliament] ⁠⁠convenes and before its committees are formed,” said Asher.
“A caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran,” he added.
Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government’s caretaker status raises the “political burden of proof”.
“Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government,” he said.
On Wednesday, Israeli media reported that the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu had ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran.
“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.
That followed reports that Netanyahu has been repeatedly calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran, conversations that on at least one occasion became heated, according to Israel’s Ynet News site.
On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying that Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation. But the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) later dismissed the reports, telling Al Jazeera they were “mere speculation”.
According to Israel’s Channel 13, the Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran. It said that assessment had been presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next government, during a briefing on Wednesday.
The opposition has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any military action unless it is critical.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, a member of the opposition bloc, said the prime minister’s caretaker government must not “make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full agreement of all security officials”.
Eisenkot echoed this sentiment in a letter to Netanyahu on Wednesday, saying that deploying Israeli forces “without a direct and immediate threat that cannot wait could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in the institutions of government”.
The Israeli premier responded by insisting the government makes all decisions based only on “security considerations”.
There would be serious divisions.
“Obviously, those who voted for Netanyahu and parties from his coalition would be in favour, while most of those who supported the so-called change bloc would be upset at Netanyahu’s use of the war to try to remain in power and block their electoral success,” said Gordon.
But ultimately, he said, most people who voted against Netanyahu’s bloc would “rally around the flag” if he resumes hostilities.
Jabareen agreed that Israelis would likely rally if a new war breaks out and missiles are incoming. But he said that “tells you very little about whether they think Netanyahu was right to start another round [of conflict]”.
“And the harder test comes when reservists are called up again, families are back in shelters and the government has to explain what the campaign can achieve that the previous one didn’t,” he added.
Jabareen said the debate in Israel over any new confrontation on Iran would likely centre on “why now?”
“If the case for urgency is weak, especially if Washington is opposed and senior Israeli commanders have reservations, the decision could be seen as an attempt to change the political agenda while Eisenkot is trying to form a government,” he said.
Beyond domestic considerations, an obstacle to Netanyahu restarting attacks may be the position of Israel’s main ally, the US, which has said it is doubling down on its economic pressure campaign against Iran rather than pursuing more large-scale military action.
“Netanyahu’s problem … is not the Israeli public, but what seems to be a loss of appetite in the US,” said Gordon.
Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said it would be easier for Netanyahu to pull off a new military campaign if it is undertaken jointly with the US.
But “the more openly Netanyahu provokes Iran, and the less support he receives from Trump, the harder it will be for him to get away with it – and for the Israeli public to accept it”, Persson told Al Jazeera.
Yes. And in one case, the government was led by Netanyahu himself.
In May 2021, weeks after his party lost seats in legislative elections and while negotiations for a new government were under way, the prime minister launched an 11-day war in Gaza that killed at least 260 people in the Palestinian enclave. Thirteen people also died in Israel.
While that conflict temporarily stalled efforts to replace Netanyahu, a new government, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was formed the following month, ending a 12-year run as prime minister .
Former Israeli prime ministers Ehud Olmert and Yair Lapid also ordered military action in Gaza while serving in a caretaker capacity. The 2008 war directed by Olmert was by far the most deadly , killing about 1,400 Palestinians.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Set to Recoup Some Losses After Huang's Exit — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Set to Recoup Some Losses After Huang's Exit — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of at least two affairs.
It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower.
Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia.
Huang was already under scrutiny following an investigation by the board into his relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Shares of Nvidia were 1.7% higher as of 8:13 a.m. ET.
Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that his departure could cost Nvidia as much as 20% of its market value, given how critical he has been to the company's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month.
A lot of the company's success has been built around Huang, said Stephane Houri, head of equity research at ODDO BHF.
It's about more than just Nvidia, but also about the "architecture of the AI industry that really depended on the vision" and expertise of Huang, Houri told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.

articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal.
But the Commerce Department is in charge, "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box."
The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed.
Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.
Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room.
Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room."
But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s."
"And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate ally before resigning as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal Thursday morning, had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.

articles.title_orig: What we know about the global Microsoft outage
articles.title_zh: What we know about the global Microsoft outage
articles.content_orig:
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products.
Efforts to completely resume services remain ongoing.
Microsoft said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.
The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.
The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.
The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.
In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.
On Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.
The company added it is focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" and warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue".
In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming for some, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.
"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

articles.title_orig: Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years
articles.title_zh: Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years
articles.content_orig:
Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.
The producer price index , which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.
Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.
On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.
The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.
Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.
Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.
The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI.
However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal.
"Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.
Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.
"We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way."
Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.
Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.
Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.
"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks."
Other items in the PPI report also showed multiyear gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

Chipmaker sector stocks declined further.
Oil prices were little changed, providing some relief after a spike in prices sparked Thursday's sell-off in bonds. As traders braced for an interest rate hike in December, the 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) reached 5.16% on Friday, its highest level since October.
The setup has pressured the price of bitcoin ( BTC ), with the world's largest cryptocurrency tumbling below $70,000 early Friday for the first time in nearly three months.

Yahoo Finance's Paige Oamek reports:
Richemont stock opened more than 4% lower on Friday morning as the Swiss luxury group reported slower growth in its jewelry business.
The owner of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels posted first-half net profit of 2.5 billion euros (approximately $2.76 billion), up from 1.8 billion euros ($2 billion) a year earlier and above analyst forecasts of 2.26 billion euros ($2.5 billion).
But eyes were on jewelry, the group's growth engine, where sales rose 14%, short of the 16% analysts had expected, according to an RBC poll.
Many luxury brands have struggled amid foreign conflicts, rising gold prices, and cost-sensitive consumers. The luxury sector has fallen some 30% in 2026, per Barron's.
Wholesale inflation data came in better than expected for the month of October, but the long-term trend painted a worrying picture of rising prices.

However, over the last 12 months, the index for final demand increased 6.5% in October, the largest annual increase since November 2022.
That keeps the pressure on the Fed to raise interest rates next month.
Fed governor Michelle Bowman said Tuesday that rate hikes may be needed to slow the pace of price increases, Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reported.
"Inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening," Bowman said in a speech in Washington.

Investors were also watching the 10-year Treasury yield, which climbed to 5.10% Thursday.
The bull market won't have it easy in 2027, Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports. According to Goldman Sachs strategist Kamakshya Trivedi, the vibes around AI investments are weakening.
Here's what Trivedi had to say about risks to stocks:
"Although we expect solid AI investment growth to continue, our forecasts imply that the investment growth impulse — additional AI investment as a share of GDP — will peak in early 2027. From a macro perspective, this should be a manageable event. But it may be a bigger test for markets for three reasons."
"First, the AI impulse has been a much larger contributor to growth in earnings and market value than to growth in GDP," Trivedi explained.
"Second, AI-related equities have taken credit for significant macro productivity gains, especially companies benefiting directly from the infrastructure boom, that have made them more vulnerable to any signs that we are on a less optimistic path," Trivedi added.
"Third, the point at which growth rates peak (a "second derivative" turning point) often matters, even if underlying growth rates (the "first derivative") remain healthy. Moving through that peak allows markets to place limits on the upside of an uncertain distribution and, as growth decelerates, the period of positive surprises to expectations often ends too, as we may be starting to see for the AI capex cycle."
Cerebras Systems ( CBRS ) stock jumped 13% in premarket trading after the AI chipmaker reported record third quarter revenue and raised its full-year outlook.

The company also announced commercial deals with two new hyperscalers, or large cloud computing providers that operate data centers. One is among the world's top three, with Cerebras saying it would share more details about the deal next year.
"These new deals, alongside continued growth and execution with our existing customers, enable us to raise Q4 core guidance across the board and continue to see revenue tripling in 2027 with expanding gross margins," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman said during the company's earnings call on Thursday.
The cheapest way for an American company to run AI is a free model made in China. The scandal that just cost Nvidia its CEO could shut off the chips those models depend on, Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre writes.
Companies are making the switch fast. Duolingo ( DUOL ) co-founder and CEO Luis von Ahn said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday that each AI practice call in his app used to cost about 30 cents. Now it's "less than a cent," he said, "by moving most of this to open weight models ," the kind of AI anyone can download and run for free. Decagon co-founder and CEO Jesse Zhang said new customers at his AI startup run "almost entirely" on them.
The most downloaded of those free models come from China, and the biggest maker by far is Alibaba ( BABA ).
Jensen Huang is out. The former CEO of Nvidia resigned after a rapid succession of damning news reports revealed multiple affairs, including one with a woman that US intelligence says is a Chinese spy and others with employees. The scandal is unequivocally damaging for Huang. And, at least in the short term, destabilizing for Nvidia, and detrimental to the AI trade , Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The key-person risk extended to the entire AI trade. Huang was everywhere, seemingly… If Nvidia was the "central bank of AI," Huang was the chair.
But if Nvidia and the broader AI trade successfully weather the storm , it could amount to a huge win for both the company and sector.
