articles.title_orig: Russia hit by second car bomb in as many days as peace talks continue
articles.title_zh: Russia hit by second car bomb in as many days as peace talks continue
articles.content_orig:
A car bomb in Moscow has injured a former adviser to Ukraine's pro-Putin ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.
Sergei Zavorotny was behind the wheel when the explosion happened on Friday morning. He was taken to hospital, investigators added.
Zavorotny had been an aide to Azarov until the prime minister resigned in 2014 and fled to Russia. The car bomb went off a day after a similar explosion killed a Russian colonel in Saint Petersburg.
It comes against a backdrop of peace talks in Dublin aimed at ending the war, although strikes by both Russia and Ukraine continued overnight.
"Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Prime Minister of Ukraine Mykola Azarov, who was driving a car, was injured. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care," a statement from the committee said on Telegram.
"A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."
Unconfirmed reports from Russia claim he has lost his left arm and suffered a brain injury, broken ribs and right leg.
On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of Saint Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military.
Russia say the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.
Overnight Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.
Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.
They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.
Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.
And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.
Ukraine say these are retaliatory attacks over Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.
This week has seen informal peace talks in Dublin at a military airbase.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff earlier had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
On Thursday in Dublin, Kushner said Putin was willing to accept European input in the peace process .
On Friday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said that European voice could not be confined to just member states - paving the way for the UK to have a role.
Ahead of an informal meeting of the EU Council, he said: "The discussions today will focus perhaps both on the content and the type of peace that Europe wants to secure, the sustainable peace, and then also in terms of there will be discussion, obviously, in terms of who represents Europe."
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has welcomed the pledge of European involvement.
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and about a fifth of the country is now under occupation.
Continued efforts to broker peace have failed so far, despite intensive talks.
On Thursday Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that UK national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join Zelensky, Witkoff and Kushner for talks in Dublin.
But hours later Downing Street said they had been delayed, which meant that the national security adviser could no longer join the meetings.

articles.title_orig: Alice Huang-Linked Firm Procured Banned Nvidia Chips in China
articles.title_zh: Alice Huang-Linked Firm Procured Banned Nvidia Chips in China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The cheapest way for an American company to run AI is a free model made in China. The scandal that just cost Nvidia its CEO could shut off the chips those models depend on.
Companies are making the switch fast. Duolingo ( DUOL ) co-founder and CEO Luis von Ahn said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday that each AI practice call in his app used to cost about 30 cents. Now it's "less than a cent," he said, "by moving most of this to open weight models ," the kind of AI anyone can download and run for free. Decagon co-founder and CEO Jesse Zhang said new customers at his AI startup run "almost entirely" on them.
The most downloaded of those free models come from China, and the biggest maker by far is Alibaba ( BABA ).
Economist Nouriel Roubini says China's edge rests on two shortcuts that are closing fast. Chinese open models are about 95% as good as American ones, the NYU Stern professor emeritus said at Invest, because "we allowed distillation — that's over — and we allowed them through Singapore to get all these advanced chips." Distillation is when one AI model learns by copying a stronger model's answers.
Alibaba stock fell 7% Thursday to its lowest close since January 2025 as reports circulated that Washington is moving to shut down that Singapore route. The company reports earnings Nov. 19.
Alibaba's free AI models, called Qwen, get about half of the downloads that can be traced to a maker on Hugging Face , the biggest online library of AI models, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's more than twice as many as Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Meta ( META ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Nvidia ( NVDA ) combined.
"Right now there is massive usage of ... a Chinese family called Qwen, which is the most used one," Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf said on Deirdre Bosa Live this week.
Meta used to own this race. Its Llama 4 and Alibaba's Qwen3 came out the same month in 2025. Developers have since downloaded Qwen3 more than 20 times as often on Ollama, a popular app for running AI on your own computer.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after admitting to an affair with a woman US intelligence officials believe passed information to Beijing, according to reports . She has been identified as Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company that rents out computing power built on Nvidia chips.
Alibaba was Megaspeed's founding customer and is still its biggest, the Financial Times reported . The US investigation targets Megaspeed, not Alibaba, and Megaspeed denies diverting chips.
China can't legally buy Nvidia's most advanced chips, so renting them abroad has been the workaround. Now the Commerce Department is finalizing a rule that would bar Chinese AI companies from using advanced chips in data centers outside China, including in Singapore and Malaysia, The Information reported .
The scandal also cost America's open-source AI its loudest booster. "Jensen was a great champion for open weight," Zhang said, adding that "there's still a gap between the open-source frontier in the US and in China." And China hawks in Washington now have an opening to press their case.
Roubini thinks Washington's crackdown will flip that gap. Without copying American models and without the Singapore chips, he said, China's AI makers are "going to lag behind us."
Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.

articles.title_orig: France slams Israel’s ‘demagogic’ ban on opposition leader Melenchon
articles.title_zh: France slams Israel’s ‘demagogic’ ban on opposition leader Melenchon
articles.content_orig:
Paris has condemned Israel’s “demagogic decision” to bar French opposition figure Jean-Luc Melenchon from entering the country.
Late on Thursday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot slammed Israel’s earlier announcement that Melenchon, leader of the France Unbowed party (La France Insoumise), was not welcome.
Israel barred the party’s parliamentary group chair Mathilde Panot, alongside Melenchon, due to the “extreme anti-Israel stance” of the party and “outrageous statements” made by its leaders.
“This demagogic decision, coming from a government that has repeatedly violated international law, plays into the hands of those who, like La France Insoumise, make a living out of exploiting the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” Barrot, who belongs to the centrist ruling coalition, wrote on social media.
“France will continue tirelessly to work toward a two-state solution and peaceful coexistence between the Israeli and Palestinian peoples,” the minister added.
Israel accused Melenchon and Panot of making “blood libel” statements against Israel.
At the weekend, Melenchon had said that if he was victorious in the upcoming presidential election in April 2027, he would order French ships to escort flotillas taking aid to Gaza.
The Israeli military has previously raided such fleets and detained activists.
“Israel will respond firmly to those who seek to harm it and will not allow individuals who act against Israel and incite against its citizens to enter the country,” a statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry said.
Speaking to French radio, Melenchon said that he had been “banned from entering a territory I did not ask to enter”.
The Israeli move came after France barred a prominent Israeli settler last week.
Yossi Dagan, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, who heads one of six Israeli regional councils in the occupied West Bank, was denied permission to enter France after landing at Charles de Gaulle International Airport.
France’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that Dagan was barred “due to his active role in implementing Israel’s settlement policy,” which violates international law.
France was one of several European countries this year to step up restrictions on Israeli settlers, spurring outrage from Israeli officials.
Earlier this year, France banned far-right Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are both members of Netanyahu’s cabinet and have encouraged accelerated settlement in the West Bank and pogroms targeting Palestinians.

Oops, something went wrong
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee was hopeful inflation would be cooling down by now. Instead, Tuesday's hotter-than-expected October inflation report marked the second straight month of rising prices — putting the central bank in what Goolsbee warns is a "precarious moment."
"I was hopeful that we were going to actually see a substantial shrinking of the inflation rate as we rolled through the tariffs and as maybe the price of oil was going to come back down, but it hasn't really worked out that way," Goolsbee said at Yahoo Finance Invest. "So we're at a precarious moment."
Goolsbee pointed to specific areas of the Consumer Price Index — including services and healthcare — that are showing persistent price pressures unrelated to tariffs or oil.
"It's worth being sober-minded at a moment like this that we're inching our way into a territory that's historically a tough spot for any central bank to try to get rid of that inflation," he said. "We'd do well to try to prevent it from getting worse."
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, compared with expectations of 0.3%, marking a slight cooldown from September's 0.6% gain. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, compared with expectations of 0.2% and unchanged from September.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Right now, the Fed is trying to untangle two competing drivers of sticky inflation: supply-side shocks, like tariffs and high oil prices lasting longer than expected, along with demand-side overheating fueled by the massive data center build-out.
While Goolsbee noted that inflation tied to AI hasn't spilled over into the broader economy yet, he stressed that policymakers are watching closely for signs that it might.
"We've got to keep an eye on that," he said. "Those are the kind of things that you'd expect to see if we were getting old-fashioned demand overheating."
Even the recent wave of newly elected Democratic governors campaigning on data center moratoriums isn't something Goolsbee views as immediately relevant to the Fed's inflation fight. For now, he sees the boom as largely contained.
"I believe most of the data center build-out has largely kind of stayed in the AI and tech lane and the adjacent industries," he said. "If that starts jumping out of its lane and overheating the economy overall, that's when we've got a problem."
Following the fresh inflation data, markets are now pricing in a roughly 90% chance the Fed hikes by 25 basis points next month, with a 10% chance officials raise by 50 basis points.

articles.title_orig: Widespread Microsoft Outage Roils Businesses, Governments and More
articles.title_zh: Widespread Microsoft Outage Roils Businesses, Governments and More
articles.content_orig:
Police forces, hospitals, GP surgeries and councils across the south of England have been sharing advice and updates after a global Microsoft outage left them without email access.
Most say they are continuing to operate as normal but some online forms and electronic-based services are not working and there may be delays to enquiries.
The region's three police forces - Hampshire & Isle of Wight, Thames Valley and Dorset - all said their phone lines were working and they were able to respond to emergencies but their online reporting systems were down.
Hospitals have asked outpatients to attend booked appointments, adding there was no need to check they were going ahead.
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems" .
Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues on Friday had so far been unsuccessful.
In a Facebook update on Friday morning, Dorset Police said: "We are currently unable to receive online form submissions. Until this is resolved, if your report is time-critical but not an emergency, please dial 101.
"If your report can wait until Microsoft restores its service, please submit an online form once you are able to do so."
Hampshire police sought to allay fears about the effect of the outage on services.
It said: "We can confirm that our ability to answer and respond to 999 and 101 calls has not been impacted by the widely reported issues with Microsoft.
"We know that the current situation will be causing concern... but our ability to respond to emergencies has not been compromised."
Isle of Wight NHS Trust said its emergency services remained operational through the outage and teams had "established plans in place to minimise disruption and maintain safe patient care".
It said: "If your enquiry is urgent, please contact the relevant service by telephone rather than email where possible."
Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said: "Our services remain operational, but there may be delays in responding to enquiries.
"If you need to contact us, please telephone us rather than email.
"If you have an appointment with us, please attend as planned. There is no need to contact us to confirm your appointment."
Tower House GP surgery in Ryde said the outage could affect some of its services, with delays responding to online consultations, hospital letters and discharge documents.
It said it was prioritising urgent clinical matters and patient safety.
Slough Borough Council in Berkshire said staff at its customer service centre who usually dealt with email enquiries had been transferred onto the phones but urged people only to call if their request was urgent because lines were expected to be busy.
East Hampshire District Council said its emails were down but residents registered on its MyEHDC system could still use the general enquiries form.
Lyme Regis Town Council in Dorset said it was using a mobile phone number for urgent issues because its telephone lines were also affected and working intermittently.

articles.title_zh: Moscow tells Europe to pick an envoy if it wants a seat at the table
articles.content_orig:
A rapid-reaction security force was assembled and put in place to secure a meeting in Dublin between Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy and US envoys on Thursday night.
Garda and Defence Forces sniper teams, as well as anti-drone professionals, worked alongside US and Ukrainian security personnel.
The meeting, which took place at short notice at the Air Corps Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, was between Zelenskiy and US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said 200 Garda personnel were on anti-drone duties, and had equipment capable of taking drones out of the skies. Some were diverted to Baldonnel for the US-Ukraine meeting, which was not known about in advance, while the Defence Forces also had an anti-drone capability on site.
“It came at very short notice, we weren’t aware of it,” Kelly said of the meeting.
Read more from Security and Crime Editor Conor Lally here .
Some “family photos” from today’s summit are coming in from our photographer Alan Betson.
Hungary’s prime minister Péter Magyar poured a pint of Guinness in Dublin after Thursday’s European Political Community summit.
Munka után édes a pihenés. Sláinte @magyarpeterMP ! pic.twitter.com/HJvCihfmDI
German chancellor Friedrich Merz has pleaded for US president ​Donald Trump to create “no surprises” during expected ​talks about Ukraine next ⁠week with Russian president ‌Vladimir ‌Putin ​in China.
“Some here in Dublin ⁠fear ​this could ​turn into a ‘second Anchorage ‌moment’,” said Merz ​on the sidelines ⁠of Friday’s meeting ​of EU leaders.
“I therefore want to state our message to the United States very ‌clearly: please, ⁠no surprises. Continue to play ‌as part of ‘Team Europe’ ​and ‘Team Ukraine’.” - Reuters
A special “VIP escort” to Dublin Airport for an individual requiring specialist medical treatment abroad was carried out “at the height of the arrivals” of heads of state and government on Wednesday.
In a statement on Friday, An Garda Síochána said it assisted in the “time-critical medical transfer”, which saw an individual transported to the UK for treatment.
The incident, which occurred as leaders were arriving for the European Political Community (EPC) summit, was managed from the Dublin regional control centre and involved a multi-agency response.
An ambulance was dispatched to collect the individual and was met and escorted “across the country” by gardaí.
“Despite the demands for EPC-related escorts in the Dublin region, a national escort motorcycle team was diverted to meet the medical escort approaching Dublin and complete this VIP escort to Dublin Airport,” the Garda said.
On arrival at Dublin Airport, the individual was transferred to a waiting HSE private air transport service which brought them to the UK.
“From first phone call the patient arrived at the required medical facility in the UK within 4 hours, well within the target window for treatment,” the Garda said.
The EU’s top foreign policy official Kaja Kallas has suggested that she should be the European voice at negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.
Following a meeting last night between Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, and Volodymyr Zelenskiy, in which Donald Trump’s envoys said a European delegate will join the next round of peace talks, Kallas said she is mandated to be the one at those negotiations.
“In 2024, in June, there was a decision by the leaders, who is representing us when it comes to security and foreign policy, and it was the discussion that in these five years there’s going to be a negotiation with Russians. So, if the leaders want to change that agreement, of course they may because it’s the leaders’ decision,” she said.
Kallas added that “all the member states actually agreed that I’m the one who is representing Europe in foreign and security policy”.
The former Estonian prime minister also believed Russia does not want her at the talks.
“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but do we have a say who is representing Russia? No, we don’t, and really we have to have a strong team,” she said.
“They don’t want anybody strong on the other side because they want to push through their maximum demands, like they have always done. - PA
Russia would be ‌open to European countries taking part in Ukraine ​peace talks if it saw that they were ready to contribute to ​the peace process, the Kremlin ‌said on Friday.
The comment suggests Russia ⁠has not yet committed to including ‌Europeans ‌in ​the next round of talks, despite US negotiators ⁠saying on ​Thursday that president ​Vladimir Putin had agreed to ‌their participation.
Asked if negotiations ​would resume in the near ⁠future with European ⁠representatives ​joining those from Ukraine, Russia and the US, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters:
“Once we understand their genuine intention and readiness to contribute to ‌the peace process, ⁠then it will be possible to make a decision ‌on holding dialogue on a Ukrainian ​settlement in an expanded format.” - Reuters
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff gave direct assurances to senior European security officials that they can join the next round of Ukraine peace talks during a meeting in Baldonnel last night.
Europe Correspondent Jack Power has gleaned some details from the shuttle diplomacy that played out at the Dublin military airbase yesterday.
It is understood that after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy sat down with Trump’s envoys, Kushner and Witkoff then held a meeting with several senior officials from Europe’s big military powers.
France, Germany, the UK, Italy and Poland had people in the room. Ursula von der Leyen’s top adviser Bjoern Seibert joined as well.
The Europeans had travelled to Abu Dhabi earlier in the week as well, where they held discussions on the margins with the US envoys and the Ukrainians, but weren’t invited to join the “trilateral” talks involving Ukraine, Russia and US negotiators.
The discussion between the US envoys and European officials in Dublin gave a clear commitment that Europe would have a seat at the table in the next round of negotiations about a settlement ending the Ukraine war. The talks will shift from a trilateral to a “multilateral” format. Though whether that’s a permanent shift is an open question.
The date of that meeting will be fixed soon, but we don’t expect to have it set before European countries who make up the “coalition of the willing” supporting Ukraine meet in Berlin next Thursday.
European leaders are still some distance apart on the idea of appointing a single representative or negotiator to speak for the EU, or the wider Continent’s interests in the negotiations.
The informal meeting of the 27 EU leaders is currently under way.
Today’s talks will focus on AI and the Ukraine war.
A bit of EU summit trivia from Jack Power :
There will be one prime minister in the room speaking for three countries on Friday.
Luxembourg’s man, Luc Frieden, is also representing the Netherlands and Belgium.
Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten couldn’t make the Dublin trip. He had to stay home for emergency talks to prevent the collapse of his minority centrist coalition.
Belgium’s Bart De Wever also sent his apologies as he’s locked in make-or-break budget talks with his coalition colleagues.
There’s a convention that when a leader can’t attend an EU summit they will nominate another head of government to speak for them. There’s no subs at this level, meaning a deputy prime minister can’t step in.
That’s why Frieden will be making the talking points for all three of the Benelux countries.
There’s no sense that the global Microsoft outage is causing major headaches for the EU summit, Jack Power writes. The leaders are set to spend the day locked in talks that maybe ironically will cover tech policy, specifically AI, its risks and opportunities, as well as the Ukraine war.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang didn’t show confidence in his successor, report says
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang didn’t show confidence in his successor, report says
articles.content_orig:
Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang described Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who has now replaced him as interim CEO, as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation earlier in the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing an anonymous source.
Huang made the comment during a meeting with Nvidia’s finance team about the company’s plans to provide guarantees worth billions of dollars to data center operators that couldn’t afford to buy its chips upfront, according to the report.
He reportedly also said Kress was a person who couldn’t help him steer strategy or decision-making.
Kress has been with Nvidia for over 13 years now, after serving as SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance. The report said she has questioned Nvidia’s program-focused, credit-based deals involving Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez, and wanted to know how to decide which deals are beneficial, how to value guarantees, and determine returns.
Earlier in the year, she had scaled back on Nvidia’s commitment for OpenAI’s ambitious Ohio data center project. The company was in talks to provide $250 billion in credit to OpenAI, but ended up committing $105 billion .
Huang resigned Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs , including one with the company’s VP for healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The company is also investigating a possible Chinese espionage plot .
After his resignation, Reuters reported that he was having a third affair with another employee . Nvidia is currently searching for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, who had the top job for over 33 years.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft says November security updates cause printing issues
articles.title_zh: Microsoft says November security updates cause printing issues
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft warned customers earlier this week that the November 2026 security updates may break printing for documents with complex formatting.
As the company explained in a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects users attempting to print documents with images that have zero height or width on server (Windows Server 2016 or later) and client (Windows 10 or later) devices.
"After installing the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), or later updates, printing might fail for documents containing images rendered with a height or width value of zero at the selected printing resolution," Microsoft said.
"These images can be used as part of certain complex document formatting, such as adding "invisible" images intended to serve as a document watermark, layout anchoring, or generation tools that may inserting images objects even when no graphic present."
The bug mainly affects users printing Microsoft Word documents via the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but it may also trigger failures when printing from other applications.
Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text , and the second broke the 'Print to PDF' feature .
More recently, the company notified customers that the August 2026 .NET Framework cumulative updates broke printing and PDF export in apps that use the Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) UI framework.
This week, Microsoft also confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates trigger Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday cause SQL Server performance and stability issues .
Additionally, the company warned that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update.

articles.title_orig: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Sells 5 Million in Four Days, Yet Former Nintendo Leads Say The Series Sold “Like Nothing” Before Breath of the Wild
articles.title_zh: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Sells 5 Million in Four Days, Yet Former Nintendo Leads Say The Series Sold “Like Nothing” Before Breath of the Wild
articles.content_orig:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has become a smashing success, selling over 5 million copies in only four days of availability, but the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of one of the best games ever released had the real risk of never seeing the light of day. According to former Nintendo of America marketing leads Kit Ellis and Krysta Yang , the franchise was going through its darkest days before the launch of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild , with new games selling like nothing.
"The series was in dire straits. They were selling like nothing," said Yang during the latest episode of the Kit & Krysta Podcast . "Yeah, I remember I was going to the focus groups. It was a really dark moment," added Ellis . "The feedback is the fan base is dwindling, this is not bringing in new players. We had so much data of like every game, the interest in the audience was getting smaller and smaller. They had to do something drastic."
Looking at the timeline, it's very likely that The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword contributed a lot to the dark age of the franchise, which required the massive open-world overhaul of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild . The first 3D entry in the series built from the ground up for the Wii system sold only 3.67 million units, a disappointing figure considering the 101 million Wii systems sold worldwide. Making this figure even more dire is how the Nintendo Switch HD remaster released in 2021 outsold the original in just a few months, benefiting from the massive popularity of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild .
With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake enjoying such incredible popularity, it will be interesting to see where Eiji Aonuma and his team will take the franchise. While both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom are incredible games, they can sometimes feel too big, a feeling that's highlighted well by the immaculate pacing of the Ocarina of Time remake, granted by the great design of Hyrule . Regardless of which direction will define the next era of the franchise, there's no denying that the dark days are indeed over for Link and Zelda .
About the author : Francesco De Meo has been covering video games and technology since 2012, starting his career at small outlets like Gamersyndrome and GeekSnack. 

After joining the Wccftech gaming section in 2015, he quickly expanded his video gaming coverage with in-depth reporting, interviews with iconic industry figures such as Grasshopper Manufacture founder and No More Heroes creator Goichi "Suda51" Suda, Resident Evil series creator Shinji Mikami, Team NINJA's president and Nioh series director Fumihiko Yasuda, and Silent Hill creator Keiichiro Toyama, reviews and on-the-ground coverage of major industry events such as Gamescom and E3.

When he's not reporting or reviewing, Francesco can be found playing the genres he loves most, spending time with his six cats, reading, writing music, playing guitar and drumming for his progressive rock band.

articles.title_zh: Gold Holds Drop to Near One-Year Low as Rate-Hike Bets Increase
articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) - The gold market is trying to attract some bullish momentum as it tests initial resistance at $3,900 an ounce, but analysts warn investors that the precious metal could continue to struggle as inflationary pressures remain a threat to the economy.
Analysts note that elevated producer prices continue to signal that inflation will remain persistently high for the foreseeable future.
The U.S. headline Producer Price Index (PPI) increased 0.3% in October, following September’s revised 1.4% increase, the U.S. Labor Department announced Friday. The latest headline data was slightly cooler than expected, as economists had forecast a 0.4% increase.
However, annual inflation continues to climb. The report said that producer prices increased 6.5% over the last 12 months, the largest annual rise since the 7.4% increase recorded in November 2022.
Higher prices are also becoming more deeply embedded in the broader economy. Core PPI, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, increased 0.3%, following September’s revised 0.8% increase. Core inflation rose in line with consensus forecasts.
Core producer prices have risen 4.9% over the last 12 months.
The gold market caught a modest bid in its initial reaction to the latest inflation data; however, the precious metal is now testing initial resistance. Spot gold last traded at $3,897.90 an ounce, up 0.57% on the day.
Although gold has been fairly resilient, analysts note that the persistent inflation threat is starting to weigh on the price action. Gold is trading near an 18-month low as rising prices is forcing the Federal Reserve to maintain its tightening bias. This week, some U.S. central bankers also voiced support for a potential 50-basis-point move next month.
Despite the ongoing risks, some market strategists see some good news in the latest PPI numbers as inflation has dropped sharply from September’s numbers.
“The headline undershot expectations and core landed squarely on forecast instead of flaring again. It’s no victory lap for the Fed, but it’s the first evidence in weeks that this week’s sticky consumer prices were the tail of the storm rather than the start of a new one,” said Artem Bakushev, Head of Risk at Monaxa.
Bakushev added that if inflation pressures start to ease, gold has room to build on its current base.
“Any hawkish pushback from Fed speakers could quickly drag it back into its range,” he said. “Investors will take this as a reprieve, not a pivot. The Fed can keep its hand off the hike lever for now, but core is still running too warm for a central bank chasing 2%. Next comes the PCE deflator, which will show whether this relief reaches the Fed’s preferred gauge and will set the tone for December’s meeting.”
Although expectations for aggressive rate hikes have grown, economists note that the latest PPI data shows no urgency for a 50-basis-point increase.
Jeffrey Roach, Chief Economist for LPL Financial, said that he expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points next month.
“While some committee members may advocate more aggressive action, we should expect a 25-basis-point rate hike. Given the fragility of the broader economy, a larger 50-basis-point increase could pose unnecessary risks,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Eleanor Donaldson given supervision order and placed on sex offenders' register
articles.title_zh: Eleanor Donaldson given supervision order and placed on sex offenders' register
articles.content_orig:
The wife of former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader and convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson has been placed under a supervision order for three years.
Appearing before Newry Crown Court, via video link, for the first time since 2025, a tearful Eleanor Donaldson was also told she would be placed on the sex offenders' register for five years.
When Judge Paul Ramsey asked if she understood that she would be subjected to a supervision treatment order (STO), she nodded her head and said "yes".
Eleanor Donaldson could not be given a prison sentence as she faced a 'trial of the facts' as it was determined she was medically unfit for a criminal trial.
She was found to have done the acts in relation to five charges, including four of aiding and abetting her husband's offending.
Last month Jeffrey Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims , including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions.
The 60-year-old appeared on screen in the court for less than three minutes, dressed in black with two large cuts on her forehead. She kept her eyes closed and head tilted down throughout.
While her husband was sentenced to 15 years in prison, Judge Paul Ramsey had four options available to him in dealing with Eleanor Donaldson under mental health legislation.
They included a hospital order, a guardianship order, absolute discharge or a supervision treatment order (STO).
It was on the advice of two medical experts that an STO was the "most appropriate" of those options. Neither the prosecution nor defence objected to this.
Judge Ramsey explained to Donaldson the terms of her STO – including that she would be under the supervision of a social worker within the Craigavon Community Mental Health Team, with whom she would be required to keep in touch, attend appointments and submit to any required treatment.
Before the judge addressed Donaldson at the conclusion of the 30-minute hearing, prosecution barrister Rosemary Walsh KC referred to victim impact statements, that spoke of anger and questions of why the offending happened.
Walsh KC said "pain permeated" through the statements of the two victims in the case.
A trial of the facts is an option that is open to prosecutors if a court determines that a person is unfit to stand trial and criminal proceedings cannot go ahead.
It takes the place of a criminal trial and is used to determine whether an accused committed the acts alleged.
It cannot result in a conviction, but if the court is not satisfied that the accused committed the acts alleged, then he/she will be acquitted.
The procedure is allowed for in legislation by Article 49A of the Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986.
The mechanism is not used often but one high-profile example was in the trial of former IRA leader Ivor Bell in 2019.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s years-long effort to get close to China
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s years-long effort to get close to China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump called Jensen Huang on Tuesday, before the Nvidia chief stepped down amid a rapidly unfolding spy scandal, and urged him to keep fighting for his job, according to two people briefed on the conversation.
The call was the latest instance of Mr. Trump defending and protecting Mr. Huang, who had become a high-profile ally and an influential adviser on artificial intelligence. The president continued to back him to the end, even after U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Mr. Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
Nvidia announced on Thursday that Mr. Huang, who built the company into the world’s leading supplier of advanced A.I. chips, had been replaced as chief executive following revelations not just of the affair with the woman suspected of being a spy, but also another with one of his employees.
A representative for Mr. Huang did not provide a comment for this article. Neither Mr. Trump nor the White House responded to requests for comment about his call to Mr. Huang.
The president had been warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a Chinese citizen known as Alice Huang, whom intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.
Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

articles.title_orig: Looking Past Nvidia Turmoil, Stocks Log Best Week in Months
articles.title_zh: Looking Past Nvidia Turmoil, Stocks Log Best Week in Months
articles.content_orig:
The stock market on Friday was set for its best week in months, as investors brushed off concerns about the resignation of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia, the behemoth chip maker.
The S&P 500 is on course to rise more than 3 percent for the week, which would be its best five-day stretch since early August. The Nasdaq Composite has also risen more than 3 percent so far this week.
The moves are an end to weeks of losses in which concerns about a slowdown in the growth of the artificial intelligence industry weighed on the market and prompted sharp sell-offs in many of the tech companies that have led the market higher in recent years.
“The market is in an incredibly good position to move higher,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for the investment management arm at Nationwide, an insurance company. “Once you get through the news-driven sentiment, you can get back to focusing on fundamentals. That is hopefully what we are seeing.”
The market was on edge after revelations that Mr. Huang, a standard-bearer for the A.I. revolution , had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
After reports that Mr. Huang had a second affair, this time with a subordinate employee, Nvidia’s board announced the chief executive’s departure on Thursday morning, a dramatic fall from grace for the tech mogul. Nvidia’s shares dropped on Thursday, and its stock is now about 30 percent below its all-time high, set just over a month ago. The company, which is the second-largest member of the S&P 500 index, behind Apple, is trading about 12 percent lower for the year.

articles.title_orig: How the Microsoft outage has been felt worldwide
articles.title_zh: How the Microsoft outage has been felt worldwide
articles.content_orig:
At least 74 countries have been affected by the Microsoft outage since it was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, were experiencing "connectivity problems", the company said.
As of 12:00 GMT on Friday, it reported seeing "encouraging recovery progress in Europe" while Japan remained "comparatively more stable" and North America was "also improving".
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, the disruption has been widespread. Here's what's been happening around the world.
In the US , staff with the House of Representatives told Politico their work had been halted by the outage.
"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems.
OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.
Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.
Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.
The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.
"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."
In Canada , a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto had declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.
The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.
Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.
Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers may not be able to receive emails about their trips due to the outage.
Disruptions have also been reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.
In Japan , some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.
"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times .
The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.
Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".
Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.
In the Philippines , the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".
In India , the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.
People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.
"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.
Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.
Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.
China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.
Australia's spy and federal police agencies have been affected by the outage, though officials have suggested the impact is minimal.
"The impact that they are dealing with is very much on email system", the head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, Mike Burgess, told reporters.
Other Australian public service providers also confirmed they had been affected by the outage, but similarly said this was mostly limited to emails, and the BBC understands there were no major impacts across New South Wales' primary services in health, education, transport, and emergency services.
European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.
In the UK , GPs, police and pharmacies are among services affected.
Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.
A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.
"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."
Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa remain unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.
However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Called Her ‘a Deer in the Headlights.’ Now She Runs Nvidia.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Called Her ‘a Deer in the Headlights.’ Now She Runs Nvidia.
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Over three decades, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang helped propel the chipmaker’s rise into one of the world’s most valuable and resilient companies, leading the business through near-death and periods of reinvention.
Now the self-described “battlefield CEO” faces a personal crisis that will test a roughly $4-trillion Silicon Valley powerhouse that has become the face of the artificial intelligence revolution.
Over the weekend, the 63-year-old tech billionaire and married father of two sent an apology to his employees, admitting he had an affair and is hoping to win back trust. Nvidia’s board announced it is launching an investigation after allegations surfaced that Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
“Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence,” Huang said in the note to employees.
The board said it doesn’t believe the relationship compromised Nvidia’s secrets or national security. China has dismissed the allegations as an unsubstantiated “smear” campaign against the country.
The revelations, though, rattled Silicon Valley and Washington, where federal lawmakers have called for an investigation into accusations that China targeted the powerful tech mogul. The scandal also comes as the U.S. competes with China in the AI race, raising more scrutiny over Nvidia’s business with the country.
Nvidia launched the investigation after the New York Times first reported in late October that American intelligence agencies found that Huang developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen that was passing on intelligence to Beijing. The woman, Alice Huang, worked as an executive for Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which is one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed didn’t respond to a request for comment but told the New York Times that it “cannot respond to a media trial and welcomes formal, evidence-based investigation.”
On Monday, Nvidia’s share price fell about 5% to roughly $177  as investors expressed anxiety about how the scandal will affect the company’s future.
Though analysts say it’s unlikely that Huang will be ousted as chief executive and Nvidia will probably remain a dominant AI player, the drama has raised questions about the company’s succession plans and how it will affect the chipmaker’s competition with rivals.
“He’s become a tech celebrity, which has shown to be both a blessing and a curse for companies. His conduct could raise questions about his judgment and potentially undermine some of the confidence he’s built among investors, customers and developers,” said Jacob Bourne, an eMarketer analyst.
Over the years, Huang, who’s known for donning a black leather jacket, has shown he’s a visionary, dealmaker and politically savvy, forging strong ties with President Trump. Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at Technalysis Research, said that Nvidia will likely be around for decades, but that the scandal is shining a spotlight on who will succeed Huang.
That will be hard to top. Huang’s two children work for Nvidia.
“He’s been able to turn that big personality and vision and dealmaking into this point where he is arguably the leader, certainly of the hardware side of the tech industry,” O’Donnell said. “Everything he says matters and every company wants to do deals with Nvidia.”
Huang is no stranger to navigating through turmoil, and as a leader he’s emphasized the importance of character and resilience.
Born in Taiwan, Huang spent some time in Thailand before his family sent him to the United States, where he attended a religious reform school. There, he told news outlets, he was bullied for being Chinese and even scrubbed toilets.
He met his future wife, Lori, at Oregon State University, where they were studying electrical engineering.
Huang, along with engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, founded Nvidia in 1993 at a Denny’s diner in San José,  where they envisioned building a computer chip to improve video game graphics.
In its early days, Nvidia contracted with game company Sega, but it almost went out of business by betting on the wrong approach for building graphics chips. Huang laid off employees and convinced Sega to invest $5 million in the company, avoiding bankruptcy, according to an interview he did on “How I Built This with Guy Raz.”
The company created specialized computer chips that would not only be used for gaming but also for cryptocurrency mining, AI model training and robotics.
Nvidia also partnered with OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, early, before people turned more to AI to automate tasks. In 2016, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s new supercomputer to OpenAI. As ChatGPT became more popular, Nvidia benefited from the AI boom.
“He’s been on the cutting edge of all of this for a very long time, and then the rest of the world kind of caught up with what he saw and what the industry was doing, and now of course we are where we are,” O’Donnell said.
As other tech leaders have called for a slowdown of the AI race, Huang has called for speeding up AI innovation, stating it could help improve safety. Computers, he said, are just software and not conscious.
Even as Nvidia’s prominence has grown, Huang has told media outlets he still worries the company could go out of business, though he says he’s stepped up in times of crisis.
“The perfect day is [when] we are in trouble, and you just create the worst possible condition. And Jensen, we need you to come and help us think through this,” Huang said in an interview on “How I Built This with Guy Raz.”
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive
articles.title_zh: Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive
articles.content_orig:
Kratom and related 7-OH products are widely available at gas stations, smoke shops, liquor stores and online. As early as Friday, the federal government could make some of the products illegal. Mindy Schauer/MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty Images hide caption
Tyler's opioid addiction began in his early 20s, and when he decided he wanted to quit, he used kratom leaf powders to help ease withdrawal symptoms.
Tyler, now 38, told NPR he thinks kratom helped him stop using opioids for a decade.
Tyler asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma attached to his history with drug use and addiction.
In early 2025, he saw a new product at a gas station called 7-OH. He hadn't heard of 7-OH, but said the tablets were advertised as "kratom products." He decided to try them, since the kratom powders he'd taken in the past "can be hard on your stomach," he said.
At first, 7-OH gave him a feeling of euphoria he described as similar to opioids, which "felt like a kind of a miracle," he said.
Nearly a year and a half later, he was in a rapid detox program in Michigan, where he was sedated to sleep through the withdrawals he experienced when he tried to stop taking it.
In the past few years , highly concentrated products with 7-OH — sometimes alongside other semi-synthetic opioids — have popped up online, and at many smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. They can come in the form of tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolate.
7-OH, or 7-hydroxymitragynine, is one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom, which comes from a tree in the coffee family. It's naturally found in kratom in very small amounts, and seems to act more like an opioid in the human brain than kratom leaf products. Kratom is used by some people with opioid addiction to maintain long-term recovery. Some people say it makes them feel energized or focused. Others describe the effects of kratom like those of opioids, and say it can relieve pain, feel calming or even create euphoria.
Some users of 7-OH and kratom show classic signs of addiction, researchers and policy officials say. But the products are not always clearly labeled, so it's difficult or impossible for users to know what quantity of the substances they are consuming.
"I did not know at all what I was in for. It was much more potent than I had imagined," Tyler said.
Estimates of how many people use kratom and 7-OH in the U.S. are wide-ranging. Some suggest over 5 million people have used kratom in their lifetime. David Epstein , a senior investigator at the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Intramural Research Program, says he's seen estimates of kratom use as high as 15 million. Those estimates don't usually distinguish between whole leaf kratom, 7-OH or other related products.
In the last decade, the U.S. government has attempted to restrict both kratom and 7-OH products, but strong opposition to those moves by the public and powerful advocacy groups backing the substances have kept them federally legal.
That's started to change in the last few months.
No federal actions have been taken against "traditional botanical kratom," but a new federal restriction on some 7-OH products could go into place as early as Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.
The path there has not been straightforward. In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) restricted the making and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids derived from 7-OH and other related compounds: MGM-15, MGM-16 and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI). Those compounds were listed under the Controlled Substances Act alongside the most highly restricted drugs , like heroin and LSD.
That caused backlash from kratom advocates who worried the rule would affect products with "trace amounts" of the semi-synthetic opioid, MGPI. One kratom advocacy organization, the American Kratom Association, filed a federal lawsuit on Aug. 26 against the DEA. It asked the DEA to ensure natural kratom products with traces of MGPI would remain legal.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) then issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI on Oct. 9, and the DEA changed its course. They now plan to restrict a narrower range of 7-OH and MGPI products: ones that contain higher concentrations of 7-OH and/or MGPI.
HHS and the DEA say they are not focusing on natural kratom products.
Kratom is derived from a tree in the coffee family. So-called "natural kratom," which can be taken as a powder, a capsule or a pill, among other forms, is not expected to be part of a likely federal crackdown. Yanawut/iStockphoto/Getty Images hide caption
Many people who oppose the restriction say kratom and 7-OH products have kept them away from traditional opioids, and helped them manage chronic pain, mood and mental health. Some also point to the fact that opioid deaths in the U.S. are decreasing. In 2023 alone, a KFF report found there were over 79,000 opioid deaths, and in 2024 there were 54,000.
A recent report of data from 53 U.S. poison control centers shows reports of calls related to kratom increased about 1,200% between 2015 and 2025. Chris Holstege , a physician and a professor of emergency medicine and pediatrics at the University of Virginia's School of Medicine, is one of the authors of that report. He said he and the other authors "were a bit stunned" by those findings, which do not distinguish between kratom or products like 7-OH.
The report included 233 deaths associated with kratom during 2015–2025, with 79% of those deaths involving multiple substances. The most severe outcomes were linked to people using multiple substances alongside kratom products, like opioids, stimulants and benzodiazepines.
But Holstege points out over half the reports of calls, 62%, involved people using kratom without other drugs.
The authors used data on kratom from the National Poison Data System (NPDS), which includes calls from the public, healthcare professionals or medical examiners, and medical records.
Still, there are people who report benefits of using kratom or 7-OH, said Epstein, the NIDA investigator.
NPR spoke to one mom in Delaware, Angela Wilson, 44, who said 7-OH has helped her manage excruciating chronic pain related to endometriosis, and symptoms of depression she's had since she was a teenager.
She said she's been taking 32 to 40 milligrams of 7-OH a day, split into three doses, for the last year and a half.
Wilson said kratom powders made her feel anxious and shaky, and 7-OH seems to work for her without those side effects.
"It's been truly life-changing for my family situation, my personal life," she said.
Wilson doesn't have health insurance, and said losing access to 7-OH under new restrictions would be "devastating" for her and her family.
"We're not really sure, you know, what I'm gonna do when it's not available," she said.
Epstein has also heard stories like Tyler's. He said people can become addicted or dependent — and some of his ongoing research suggests that risk is higher with 7-OH products than with whole leaf kratom.
He said for some people, their 7-OH use "seemed to go nicely for the first couple of days, but then they found that they had to keep using to avoid withdrawal," Epstein said. "And some of them, not all of them, but some of them, even said they had to, you know, they couldn't make it through the night. They had to get up in the middle of the night to take more."
He said other people were happy with the effects they got from taking 7-OH and didn't feel like it caused problems for them.
Tyler told NPR that 7-OH tablets gave him more energy at first. He works a job where he's on his feet a lot, and with 7-OH, he said, " I can go, go, go, go, go, you know?"
He began taking around 300 to 400 mg of 7-OH a day, about ten times the dose Angela Wilson takes. In the next year, he said he made a few attempts to stop, but the withdrawals were debilitating.

articles.title_orig: Ford opens massive new archive putting over a century of automotive history on display
articles.title_zh: Ford opens massive new archive putting over a century of automotive history on display
articles.content_orig:
Ford archives and heritage brand manager Ted Ryan explains how the automaker assembled roughly 150 vehicles under one roof and why its past can help inspire the future.
Ford Motor Co. is opening the doors to a massive new archive outside Detroit, bringing roughly 150 historic vehicles, concept cars and racing machines under one roof.
The 79,000-square-foot Ford Vault opens Friday and consolidates vehicles previously stored across several locations in southeast Michigan , giving employees and visitors a firsthand look at more than a century of the automaker's history.
"It's going to be a spectacular place for people to come and visit," Ted Ryan, Ford's archives and heritage brand manager, told FOX Business ahead of the opening.
The collection includes a 1910 Model T, World War II-era military vehicles, concept vehicles, a Formula One race car and a 10-cylinder Mustang, he said.
FORD UNVEILS 2027 F-150 WITH HANDS-FREE TOWING, FIRST-EVER CARHARTT EDITION
Jay Leno's 1934 Ford Model T. (Ford Motor Co..)
Ryan said Ford began building out its U.S. heritage fleet about three years ago after CEO Jim Farley pushed the company to develop a collection similar to ones it maintained overseas.
Ford ultimately gathered more than 60 concept vehicles, roughly 50 racing vehicles and dozens of others from its archives, bringing the collection to about 150 vehicles .
Previously stored across multiple locations, including the garage at Ford's former headquarters, the vehicles are now being brought together at the Vault.
Among them is a 1941 Ford GP, an early military vehicle tied to Ford's role in America's World War II industrial effort.
Ryan said Ford went on to build roughly 282,000 GPWs during the war.
FORD RECALLS MORE THAN 40,000 TRUCKS AND SUVS OVER VISIBILITY RISK
Another standout is a 1998 Stewart Formula One car, a reminder of Ford's long history in motorsports.
Other vehicles showcase some of Ford engineers' more unusual creations.
"Some of our crazy smart engineers figured out how to make a 10-cylinder car, but then how to cram it into a Mustang and a Mustang body. And so it's just insane," Ryan said.
But the Vault isn't intended only to preserve Ford's past. Ryan said the collection can also serve as inspiration for today's designers and engineers.
"It matters because to look forward, you always have to know where you've been," Ryan said.
He pointed to vehicles such as the Bronco and Mustang, saying designers can study what made earlier generations distinctive without simply recreating them.
FORD’S US MANUFACTURING EXPANSION TO BRING ‘THOUSANDS AND THOUSANDS OF JOBS,’ LUTNICK SAYS
The No. 1 Ford GT40 Mk. II of the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans.
Upon entering, visitors will be greeted by two Ford GTs and a 1910 Model T, followed by rows of vehicles spanning generations of Ford history.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
"It's just going to car after car after car, where, if someone wanted to, they could devote however much time just to do a deep dive into not just what that car meant, but Ford's role in culture and society," Ryan said. "[There are] stories within stories."
Earlier this year, Ford also put its history on display in Washington, D.C., opening a free exhibit at Union Station as part of the nation's 250th birthday celebrations.

articles.title_orig: Russia seeks Finland's NATO exit, Baltic military base ban in Ukraine talks: Report
articles.title_zh: Russia seeks Finland's NATO exit, Baltic military base ban in Ukraine talks: Report
articles.content_orig:
Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security
Europe live – latest updates
The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US were held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Despite more than two years of on-off talks, the EU has not settled on a choice. But there is a growing view that Europe should not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent.
Paris and Berlin support a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: the European Council’s president, António Costa, and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
after newsletter promotion
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing , a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the Health Ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday.
The strike hit a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, with medical staff and patients among those killed, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, health officials said. The Israeli military said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants.
The strike — the latest despite an ongoing U.S.-backed ceasefire — shattered ceilings and left debris strewn across wards inside the hospital, which is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza after the destruction of Israel’s yearslong military assault.
Palestinian surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira was among those killed, the Health Ministry said. He was featured in the 2026 documentary “American Doctor,” which followed three American doctors helping to provide medical care in Gaza.
An array of munitions debris was displayed at the hospital site as media visited on Thursday. Two munitions experts said an image supplied to NBC News appeared to show debris from a GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb. The U.S. is known to supply Israel with GBU-39 munitions, which are produced by Boeing in the United States and sold to a number of countries.
The IDF and Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether U.S.-manufactured munitions were used in the strike. While the image was captured at Nasser Hospital following the strike, NBC News is not able to independently confirm that they were the munitions used in the attack or how they came to be displayed there.
Justin Bronk, a senior research fellow for airpower and technology in the military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank based in London, said he made that determination based on the “wing section visible,” adding that the GBU-39 “is a U.S. supplied weapon.”
Brian Castner, a crisis researcher at Amnesty International, also identified the munitions as belonging to a GBU-39, adding that Israel has used the bomb “in many strikes in Gaza.”
Sam Lair, a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute who manages and conducts investigations into nuclear and missile programs, said NBC News’ imagery appeared inconclusive, but “the wings, tail actuation system, lugs, and warhead” shown in other photos appear to match “a GBU-39 series small diameter bomb.”
“It looks to be some kind of glide bomb or cruise missile, and the English on the frame suggests it could be U.S.-origin, but I don’t see anything conclusive,” he said.
Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, head of the surgery department at Nasser Hospital, said there was no “notice, warning or anything” before the hospital was attacked. “Suddenly, there was fire and shelling and walls were brought down instantly,” he said.
He said he was not aware of any “resistance fighters or combatants present — only a medical team treating patients.”
NBC News also spoke with two surgeons who travelled to Gaza from the U.K. earlier this month to assist with medical care, and were said were in the hospital when the missile struck.
Both Dr. Goher Rahbour, a consultant general and colorectal surgeon, and Dr. Stephan Verborg, a limb reconstruction surgeon, said they were also not aware of any warning from the Israeli military before the strike, which hit the hospital shortly after midnight.
“I heard the impact and I felt the explosion because the whole hospital shook,” Verborg said in a phone interview Thursday. He said he was about 15 to 20 meters away from the point of impact, adding: “You could smell the smoke. You could see the dust.”
Rahbour said he had been operating with Abu Shaira, whom he described as a “lovely” and “affable” person, earlier that day. He said they had been laughing and joking together Wednesday evening in the hours just before the Palestinian surgeon was killed.
Both doctors had traveled to Gaza early this month through the organization IDEALS, a U.K. charity seeking to provide sustainable humanitarian aid to regions affected by conflict or natural disasters. They said they had not seen any indication of a Hamas presence in the hospital.
Tributes were paid to Abu Shaira. “Dr. Rizq was at the hospital during the entire war,” Dr. Mohammed Zaqout, director general of the Health Ministry in Gaza, could be seen telling a crowd of mourners, surrounding a body covered in a shroud, in a video captured for NBC News on Thursday. “He didn’t abandon his duties for even one day.”
Nasser Hospital said a 13-year-old boy, identified as Jihad Naeem Muhammad Abu Tilikh, was also among those killed.
The Israeli military and the Israel Security Agency said they struck a senior Hamas member, along with other militants, who they said had “advanced” attacks from the hospital in the southern Gaza Strip overnight. In a later statement, they identified the senior member as Muhammad Abu Ismail, who they said served as the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade and had also been responsible for holding hostages in Gaza.
The IDF and ISA said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command center” and stored weapons and conducted interrogations and torture from within the medical complex.
The IDF claimed the hospital’s second floor “serves as a Hamas military HQ, where civilians are not permitted to enter,” alleging that “dozens of hostages were held captive” there earlier in the war. It shared undated photos of weapons that it alleged were found within the complex and others.
The IDF and ISA said steps had been taken to “mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.” They also later said “advance warnings were issued to the population.” The IDF said it was looking into reports that medical workers,  including Abu Shaira, and patients were killed.
One woman, Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza, said her brother, Khaled Abu Anza, was killed in the strike, with Nasser Hospital separately confirming his death.
A number of media outlets, including Israeli media outlet Ynet , reported that a commander in Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade of that same name was killed in the strike. Asked to confirm that and whether he was directly targeted, the IDF said it would get back on the matter.
Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza did not directly identify her brother, 53, as a Hamas member, but said she believed he was targeted. He had been at the hospital for physical therapy after undergoing surgery, she said.
“He did not come to the hospital to engage in combat or resistance. He came for medical treatment,” she said.
Hamas condemned the allegations that it was using the hospital for military operations as “lies of the criminal enemy” and called the attack a “war crime.”
Hospitals have protected status under international law, but they have been heavily targeted under Israel’s yearslong offensive in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating within medical facilities, a charge the militant group has denied.
The overnight attack was not the first time that Nasser Hospital itself has been targeted.
In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double tap Israeli strik e that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The deadly attack sparked international outrage.
Of Gaza’s 37 hospitals, just two are considered to be “fully functioning,” while 18 are partially functioning and 17 are considered nonfunctioning after much of the enclave’s healthcare system was devastated under Israel’s offensive, according to data published by the World Health Organization.
Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached in October of last year.
More than 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the enclave. Israel says four of its ⁠soldiers have ​been killed in that time.
Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
